utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can I ask the Prosecution to introduce themselves, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. I apologise for the delay on behalf of the Defence team for General Hadzihasanovic. There was a certain error. We should have had a meeting with the witness at 7.45; however, he was wrongly informed that the meeting would be at 9.45, and that was the reason that we were late. And we apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the personnel of this courtroom. Actually, we are starting with a delay of some 15 minutes. This seems to be linked to a problem that the Defence should have had a meeting with the next witness. It is true that the senior legal officer was informed that you needed 15 minutes for this meeting, but we didn't know exactly the reason for the delay. When we have this sort of problem, there are two solutions. As you are at least two on the Defence team, one can meet with the witness, while the other is present here. Or the witness could be seen during the break. So let us make sure next time that we start on time to avoid any problems. We need to render our decision on the question of a hostile witness. The Chamber first wishes to recall the procedure applied during the hearing of this witness, so that yesterday at the end of the cross-examination by the Defence the Judges put questions to the witness before the re-examination of the Prosecution. Before the re-examination started, the Prosecution requested a longer break so that they might conduct some additional inquiries and to be able to re-examine the witness after the Judges in view of the new elements that appeared during the answers to the questions put by the Judges before the break. When the hearing resumed, the Chamber was asked orally for the witness to be declared a hostile witness because the Prosecution feels that there was no way for them to produce the necessary evidence and that they had difficulty in getting precise answers to questions. That the witness was hesitant in his answers, which actually curtailed the examination-in-chief and that during the proofing session the witness had said something quite the opposite to what he said yesterday. And in connection with the Travnik barracks, he told them that there were HVO detainees and how many. He referred to beatings, whereas here in the courtroom he never mentioned those beatings. That also during the proofing he said he didn't identify any orders, that he had no part in making decisions about those orders, whereas those orders were addressed to him and his name appeared on those orders. That the witness is not telling the truth and that consequently the Prosecution is applying for permission for him to be confronted with his statement in favour of their case. On the basis of those -- in response to those grounds, the Defence said that the oral testimony does not significantly differ from his written statement and that there was no reason to declare the witness a hostile witness. The Chamber noted that the statements of the witness regarding the prisoners in the Travnik barracks appear to be in contradiction what the witness said yesterday on the transcript, 10 hours 23 minutes, 25 seconds. By way of example, he asserted that there were only BiH detainees, whereas in paragraph 14 of his written statement he mentioned that there were also HVO prisoners. And in paragraph 13 of his written statement, it is mentioned that there were facilities designed for HVO prisoners. The Chamber is of the opinion that the witness did not respond to the legitimate requests of the party calling him and that there is reason to consider him a hostile witness. Under those conditions, the Prosecution is authorised to put questions to the witness regarding the contents of his written statement. Therefore, we're going to bring the witness into the courtroom. I will give the floor to the Prosecution to put questions that they consider to be opportune in relation to the written statement. After that, I will give the floor again to the Defence who may re-examine. And if necessary, the Judges will have some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You may sit down. I need to give you an explanation why the hearing was interrupted yesterday and you were asked to stay in The Hague and to appear again this morning. During your replies to questions put to you, the legal situation arose in which you are a hostile witness, even though you were called by the Prosecution. Within this very specific procedure, the Chamber has decided that the Prosecution is going to ask you questions on the basis of the written statement that you signed on the 14th of November, 2003. In this written statement that the Chamber has reviewed, there are several points that may appear to be in contradiction with what you said yesterday in answering questions; therefore, the Prosecution is going to put a certain number of questions to you again, after which the Defence will exercise their right to cross-examine you, and the Judges may also ask you some more questions. I wish to remind you, as I did so yesterday on a number of occasions, that you have taken the solemn oath to tell the whole truth, and I wish to remind you that the Rules do envisage the possibility of prosecuting a witness providing false testimony. So I am putting you -- I'm letting you know about this. I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, to Madam Benjamin, and try to answer those questions as precisely as possible and telling the truth, the truth about -- of what you eyewitnessed, what you heard, or what you did. Madam Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Eminovic. Mr. Eminovic, on the 11th and 14th of November, 2003, you gave a statement to representatives of the Prosecution, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the interview was conducted in English. You gave the statement in English, and you signed the English statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But at my request that I sign the statement in the Bosnian language, representatives of the Prosecution -- or rather, the people I gave the statement to told me that they would let me have a Bosnian version in seven days' time. So that page number 8, where mention is made that the statement was read in the Bosnian language, was left out of my statement which I signed and which is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I am a little bit puzzled.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And perhaps, Mr. President, it would be good now for the witness to be shown the statement, please, a copy of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to the Chamber that on page 8, that the statement was supposed to be translated into the Bosnian language before you signed it. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 8, as you can see, that number 8 is written by hand. It was number 9. One page was left out. And on that page, it was stated that the statement had been read out to me in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On page 9?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That page is not here at all; it's missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I put it to you that that page is missing because there was never a page 9. Wasn't the interview conducted to you in English?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But I --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Hold on a second. Let's go one at a time. Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Was the proofing conducted in English?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When the statement was taken from you - and the interview was conducted on the 11th and again on the 14th of November -- it was completed on the 14th of November, 2003, which is just a couple of months ago - how was the interview conducted? In what language?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When the interview was finished and you gave a statement, what language did you give the statement?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When the statement was read back to you, what language was it read to you in?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you signed the statement, what language was written? In what language was the statement written?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to your position in the OG, which is paragraph 7 of the statement. Could we start with that point. Were you a member of the OG?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you at any time be a part of any military unit of any sort?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Before the war, I was at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We are not going back to the military academy. We know that you were trained in the military academy. And to just assist you along the way, yesterday you indicated that you wore two hats; sometimes you acted in the capacity of a civilian and sometimes you acted in the capacity of a military advisor.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I worked wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague mentioned that the witness had said yesterday that he was advisor. He never stated that yesterday. He just repeated what he had stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. In the interests of moving along, Mr. President, at this moment I would like to show the witness an order dated 28 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you cast your eyes to the bottom of the page, please, where you can see your name. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And next to your name, could you tell us what you see.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] "Member of operations group command."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: All right. So let's just go forward a little bit. Yesterday I asked you who was Salko Beba subordinated to. Do you recall what you told me?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No. In fact, at page 8, line 3 of the transcript you said, "Salko was subordinated to the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war." Would you like to correct it now?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it referred to the work he conducted in the Commission for Exchanges, that the question referred to that part of Mr. Salko Beba's duties. In my written statement, it's stated that as deputy commander he was responsible to the commander of operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Clearly that's what is said in paragraph 7 of the statement, but that was not your reply, as you see on page 8 on line 6, so that's why I needed to get it clarified. So now that we have it clarified, Salko Beba was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. Who did he take orders from?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For duties related to the war exchange -- exchange. He was held responsible to that body. And as regards his duties in the operations group, to the commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When we first started, if you the recall, I said to you that you were dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Yes, the Defence rose why?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that -- that it is not all right to refer to parts of the transcript if they are not in extenso presented to the witness. On page 8, line 4, it is said: "Can you inform the Chamber to whom you were subordinated when you spoke of his membership to the commission." He said that he was subordinated to Salko Beba, who is president of the exchange commission. And who was Salko Beba subordinated to?" To the state commission for exchanges. So this has nothing to do with the second part of the question put by my learned friend and which was taken note of in his written statement. We only spoke of relations within the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. At this juncture, the Trial Chamber has to intervene. We are given a document. Well, the document is submitted to the witness, who seems to be a member of the operational group, the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group. So according to this document, it looks as if this witness was a military man and he's subordinated to Mr. Beba in his capacity as a military man. It is therefore logical to ask the following question: Who is above Mr. Beba? I think that's the reason why the Prosecution put its question. Everybody has understood that there are two parts, two aspects: There is one part that is the exchange commission, which has a military and civilian part; and there is another aspect, which is totally military, a totally military one. This witness was a member of the exchange commission, and then he was also a military man; therefore, he's in a position to clarify the situation. Witness, there is a basic problem. You seem to be in full contradiction between the answers that you provide here and this document. The Prosecution has asked you whether you were a member of the operational group. You said no. You are being submitted a document where it shows or it seems that you are a member of the operational group. So what are you saying? What are you stating? Indeed, this document looks like an official document from the 3rd Corps, and it is addressed to you, and it is not addressed to a civilian person but to a military man, so what are you stating? I don't want to put you in a tough situation, to put you on the spot, but don't beat around the bush, as we say. Just answer the question directly. I told you that yesterday already. If there is a part that may be bothering you, say so; in which case the Chamber will say, "Well, you can speak and you'll be protected by some kind of immunity." The question was a very precise one. Your name is in a document that is a purely military document. So what are you saying to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is -- was drafted at the beginning when the operations group was just being formed, when it was not capable of functioning. In other documents, two other persons will appear as members of the operations group, but they were never really appointed to such positions and within the structure of the operations group. As the operations group became staffed, these persons would leave the operations group and the persons appointed by the corps command took up certain positions. To simplify matters, Salko Beba put my name as a member of the OG. I never had been officially ordered as to be appointed to the group. This is a document that needs to be issued by a superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have your written statement in front of you. Please look at paragraph number 7, which is in English, and you know English. And in English, it is stated that Beba and yourself were members of the Military Security Service. That's what you stated. So what are you saying now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this is concerned, when making this statement, I said that I had ID of the Military Security Service issued by the 3rd Corps which I had received in mid-1993 and which I returned at the end of that year. That official ID on request of Salko Beba was issued to me. And when I stopped my engagement there in the OG, this ID was returned -- that is, when the capacities were filled, my aid -- assistance was no longer required. But officially, I had an official ID and I stand by that. And I mentioned that in point 7, and I said that I was a member of the Military Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to you, your official duties came to an end when precisely? Because one has the impression that you are a military man against your will. Tell us, please, when precisely your official duties ended within the operational group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] End of 1993 fully, because at that moment the Commission for Exchanges of the 7th Corps was set up - that is to say, of the OG - and after that the offers for cooperation with the UN and other international organisations was set up in Travnik and I began working there. And in February 1994 I moved to the Ministry of the Interior fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are stating that in 1993 you had duties within the operational group; is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in the operations group, but I didn't have any specific duties. I didn't have a position in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are telling us the following: "I worked within the group without having any official position." But did it happen? Were there occasions when you carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had a weapon. What kind of a weapon? A rifle, a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that when you would go to the group in your military uniform, it meant that you also had your pistol with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My pistol -- well, I had it when I was in civilian clothes too, as a member of the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior. Sometimes I would wear it in civilian clothes; sometimes I wouldn't take my pistol when wearing military clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the military uniform that you would wear, were there insignia and what kind of insignia did it show?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no insignia. I had a badge where it said "the municipal commission for exchange of war prisoners," and that was the logo of that commission, with my name, surname, and with my position in the municipal commission. Frequently in -- when we were receiving refugees from Bosanska Krajina we would wear uniforms because we had to help people board the UNPROFOR trucks, to drag them out of ditches, and it was easier to do those kind of jobs wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, maybe I should be more explicit. I'm confining my questions to the period January 1993 to March 1994. Now, if you look at the order that is in front of you, could you tell us the date of the order.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you would agree that that is just about mid-1993; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, prior to the 28th of June, 1993 and from the beginning of 1993, which is 1st January 1993, what was your position in the OG?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the OG, I wasn't in that group until 1993. I don't really know when I started providing services there, when I started working in the OG. I would like to correct myself here: To mid-1993. Before that, I was engaged in the exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let us not go to the civilian part. Let us just stick right now to the OG part, because that is very important to us. You notice at the bottom of the page that you have that it refers to the position that you held in the OG. The bottom of the order, the page, at the bottom where your name is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You notice there's a position next to it.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here we have a membership and not a position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So are you saying that that order was drafted wrongly, that you didn't hold that capacity then?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no official appointment in the operations group. I cannot deny that I worked in the OG, that I didn't help Mr. Salko Beba [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you're absolutely sure about that? Absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President, at this time may I show the witness another order, please. And for the benefit of the Court, Mr. President, it's also on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you have the other order in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you read the date for us, please, of that order.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 4th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in particular, could you read number 4 on the order, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Jasenko Eminovic, Bosanska Krajina OG, assistant for military security, is responsible for conducting the investigating process. He shall conduct the criminal investigation with the help of members of criminal department of Bosanska Krajina OG, CVP, military police centre."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I can see on the screen - and it is being written in English and read out in English only - it is the right of my client to have the text in the Bosnian language. And so I would kindly ask to have this text submitted to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was about to ask this, and I asked myself this initially. Do you have the orders in B/C/S? You should have them, because here we have translated text and the accused should be provided with text in their mother tongues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to apologise on behalf of the Prosecution. I think it was an oversight on our part. Because the witness speaks English, we just had the English version. But certainly within a short moment we can provide the accused with the copy in his language. If my friend would want me to move on and then come back to this, I'd certainly be prepared to do that. If it's -- if it's not a problem, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You will be able to provide this when? How much time do you need? This B/C/S text, it must be somewhere. I'll give you the floor in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think within another 20 to 30 minutes before we take the break or even less. It's just to find the document and bring it down to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no objection to have the learned colleague to continue with the interrogation, but I don't think it -- I think it would be correct vis-a-vis my client to ask him whether he wishes to have the text and documents in the English language in the Serb B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break now, during which the Prosecution will have time to find the B/C/S text. And after the break, we shall resume the hearing with everybody having the text in B/C/S and with the accused having the text in B/C/S. It is five to 10.00, and we'll resume at twenty past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, has it found -- located the document in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Usher, could you please hand the document out. We have a document in B/C/S, the order of the 28th of June. Have you found that one, the order of the 28th of June? Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We also have that one. I think we are missing page 2. And since we are dealing with July 4th now, I assume page 2 will soon come and then we'll give you the package for the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then please continue with the document of the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have noticed that the English version that we received earlier on, it says that the document was signed and stamped. Now that we have received the Bosnian version, it is clear that this document is not signed and it does not have a stamp, though the words are printed saying that it is signed and stamped. However, we have checked, and this is a document that the Defence is challenging for these particular reasons. And for the benefit of the transcript, I wish to draw attention to this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin, the Defence is telling us that, contrary to the English version, this document doesn't seem to have been signed by Mr. Alagic, as there's no signature on it except for what is stated here. And maybe there is a signature. Maybe that is Mr. Alagic's signature. We don't know. But could you tell us how you obtained this document, from which archives does it come. And the Chamber notes that there is a stamp on it which seems to be an official stamp of the Motorised Brigade, "312th Motorised Brigade" it says on the stamp. Of course, I am translating on the basis of my own knowledge of the B/C/S language. Madam Benjamin, what is the source and origin of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was just a little before my time, so I think Mr. Withopf would better be able to explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it's most likely, but it has to be verified if necessary -- however, it's most likely that this is a document stemming from the Sarajevo collection. This is a document collection, as repeatedly mentioned, which was seized in October 2000. However, if the need arises, this can be verified within a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With this reservation, Madam Benjamin, please continue your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, before the break we looked at number 4. And according to you, when you read it out, it said that you are the assistant for military security. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So are you now saying that clause 7 is correct, that you were a member of the OG and in fact the position you hold was military security -- assistant for the military security?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I was a member of the Military Security Service, but I did not have any position in the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at number 4 again, could you continue reading after "assistant for military security." Could you continue reading for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fact that we have objected to this document for formal reasons, it would be normal for the discussion about the document to continue only if the witness has ever seen this document and can recognise it, rather than interpreting sentences that it contains. So I think that the proper way is for this witness to be asked whether he ever saw the witness that is being shown -- the document, sorry, that is being shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, the document shown to you in B/C/S with a stamp on it of the brigade, and it has your name on it, had you seen that document at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see this document at the time, and I said so clearly when making my statement in Sarajevo, that I don't remember being involved in those activities at all, and that was the first time for me to see this document. And I repeated this during the proofing with the Prosecution. Because those activities are mentioned in one of the paragraphs of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document that you have in front of you signed by Mr. Alagic -- you know who Mr. Alagic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If Mr. Alagic had the position that he had - because he has passed away in the meantime - if he signs an order from the 3rd Corps and mentioning your name as being in charge of the responsibility of conducting investigations concerning criminal acts committed by members of the operations group, by this order you are charged with this function. Can one imagine that the commander at the time, Mr. Alagic, could have made an order without the addressee of that order being aware of it? Is that possible, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could happen, because such things did happen, because of the activities I engaged in in the exchange commission. Very often I could not be reached because I spent most of my time working in the exchange commission. At the same time as humanitarian-aid deliveries were being organised through territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, members of the commission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am stopping you there because I wish to say the following: In paragraph 4, it is indicated within this order that you had the professional assistance of the 312th Motorised Brigade and there was a lawyer within that brigade, Gordana Zec. Imagine if the Chamber could have Madam Gordana Zec coming to the Tribunal - I don't know if she's a woman or a man - and if she tells us indeed, "I did work with Mr. Eminovic," what would be your position then? What situation would you find yourself in in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zec Gordan will certainly say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do. I do. He will say that he cooperated with me because he took part in the training sessions that I mentioned yesterday. Those are the four military policemen covered by the training. But I don't believe that Mr. Gordan Zec would say that I took part with them in these activities, because I don't remember at all being engaged for these activities. I saw this order for the first time when I was giving my statement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that this is the first time that you are seeing this order. And the other persons mentioned, Samir, Emir Hotic and Anel Cizmo, do those names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you work with those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are persons who were members of the military police company and who were part of the training that I referred to in my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have noted that this order is about the exchange of prisoners in -- notably Croatian prisoners, and you have a role in that according to point 4 of the order. Well, yesterday you said that your main job was to organise exchange of prisoners, and how can it be in that situation that you don't know about this order? Because it's the heart of your job, as you explained it yesterday to us.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I was not informed of this order. The lists of prisoners of war for exchange were drawn up on the basis of the requests of the exchange commissions of the Croatian or Serbian side. We didn't have any information as to which members of the HVO or the Army of Republika Srpska were in detention until we addressed a request to the military authorities to see whether those persons were detained, or if we received such information from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... investigation process is among soldiers of the HVO, possible crimes that they could have committed. Yesterday you told us that you were engaged in that field, that you interviewed many persons about crimes that could have been committed by Serbs or by Croatian soldiers or civilians. So that is also the question: How can it be that you don't know about this order?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I was probably not reachable at that point in time. I was probably doing something else. But believe me, the first time I saw this order was in Sarajevo, either on the 11th or the 14th of November, when I was giving my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take note of your position. Madam Benjamin, can you move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As a member of the Military Security Service, one of your duties had to do with the drafting of orders re the military police; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday on a number of occasions that I assisted Mr. Beba because he was a member of the command of the operations group, and I assisted him in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not authorised to issue orders. I couldn't sign an order. I couldn't deploy people. This was purely the administrative part of the job, putting words on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I'm putting it to you that you did so in your capacity as assistant for military security. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the Military Security Service and not as a clerk, because I was not appointed to the position --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with all due respect, we are not talking about a clerk here. We are talking about your position. And the reason why I am putting it to you is because you made the statement. And the reason why I am putting it to you is because in your position certain things you would have known of that you have denied, that you would not have known, and that is why I just want us to clarify this area before we move. And in the interests of time, I think we would have to move on because it's clear, it's in black and white. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the Prosecution can please confer for one or two minutes. We have to address the issue which has been raised by our learned friend from the Defence in respect to the document. It would only take one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you see when I look at paragraph 7 of your statement and when you look at paragraph 10 of your statement, the second line at the very end when you talk about your duty, it says, "And also orders in military service." So when we look at those two and I combine it with the order of July 4th, 1993 - and I had asked you to look at the B/C/S now - July 4th, 1993, are you looking at it, the B/C/S version? Below Mr. Alagic --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have asked the witness whether he ever saw this order before, and the witness has not once but at least five times said that he saw it for the first time during his first interview with representatives of the OTP in Sarajevo. As the witness is unable to recognise the order, it can no longer serve as a basis for the Prosecution to refer to it and to compare it with something else. I believe that the Prosecutor should be cautioned about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence was raising an issue about the document which in the English version says "Verified with stamp and signature," and she was raising the issue that there is no stamp and/or signature on the document. The Prosecution has inquired what the words at the very bottom of the document - namely, the words "ovjerno pecatom potpisom" - what these words mean, and these words mean "certified by a rubber stamp and signature." That obviously reveals that the English translation has been the correct one. And the Prosecution is a bit concerned about this procedure, since my learned colleague from the Hadzihasanovic Defence is a B/C/S speaker and she knows what these words do mean. So the English translation reflects perfectly what is written in B/C/S on this document. I wish to bring this to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you can check with the transcript. I said that there were the words in English "verified with stamp and signature," but there's no actual stamp and signature, though the words "verified with stamp and signature" are typed in. But there's no signature or stamp on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this matter, the Chamber will not dwell on it because there is the stamp of the 312th Motorised Brigade dated the 4th of July, with Alagic's signature. This authenticates the document. So I think that the B/C/S document does not require further discussion. The only thing is to see whether the witness was aware of this document. He tells us he was not. So that is that. Now the Prosecution is raising the question of paragraph 7 and 10 for their questions. The Defence appears to oppose this, but in fact paragraphs 7 and 10 are not directly related to paragraph 4 of the document that he doesn't recognise but it is a written statement when he said in paragraph 10 that in his administrative activities included writing orders, transferring prisoners of war, and making orders for the military police. So the Chamber is putting to you the following question: In paragraph 10 that you have in front of you, you said that you assisted Mr. Beba with administrative work and you specified what that work was, saying "such as writing orders, transferring prisoners of war," and it is not properly worded in English, "orders intended for the military police." Are you confirming today that in your so-called administrative activities or work which related to the operations group, you participated in the drafting - we are not saying that you signed them - but you participated in preparing and drafting orders? Do you confirm that, that you participated in drafting orders, in preparing physically or intellectually those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that I assisted Mr. Salko Beba in writing orders about the deployment of members of the military police company. This can be checked in the transcript and I stand by what I said. I did write orders, upon his instructions, regarding the transfer of individual parts of the military police company to other positions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So line 20, page 26 you're saying "I did write orders upon his instructions." So you drafted orders upon his instructions. So it's quite clear now. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have to note in the transcript, page 25, line 21 that the document of the 4th of July does bear the signature of Mr. Alagic. My colleague a moment ago mentioned that the document in question is not signed and that is the basis of our objection. I want to ask whether the Chamber has rendered a decision saying that the document is signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber finds that there is a signature at the bottom of the page with the date below it. Apparently that is Mr. Alagic's signature. But we have other documents signed by him, and it would be sufficient to compare the two, unless the Defence can tell us today that this is not Mr. Alagic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take the floor at this stage, though it is my colleague who will be doing the cross-examination, because I drafted the objections of the Defence regarding the admissibility of these documents and we actually contest the fact that this signature at the bottom of the page is Mr. Alagic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will take note of that. Mr. Withopf, perhaps regarding signatures you can bring some light to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not in respect to the signature at this point in time, Mr. President. Since, however, the issue was raised as to where and when the Prosecution got this document, the inquiries have confirmed what I said a few minutes ago; this document was seized in October 2000 from the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo. It forms part of the so-called Sarajevo collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Benjamin, you may move on. The witness just told us that upon instructions from Mr. Beba he did draft and write orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And so we're going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could we go to the Travnik barracks now. And before we start, can I ask you to confirm for me that at your proofing on the 19th of April, 2004 were you given the B/C/S version of your statement to read?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you read it?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you make any corrections, substantial corrections? Did you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several substantial corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did make several important corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. And would those corrections be different in any way from the statement that you gave on the 11th and the 14th of November, 2003?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now it is hard for me to say. If I had the document that I corrected in your presence, then I would be able to tell you, because I don't remember exactly. I know that there were certain details that were changed linked to Mr. Bonic Krunoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I am about to show it to you, because maybe we share a different opinion what "substantial" is and what --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the witness be shown his statement that was shown to him during proofing, please. The B/C/S statement, that is. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could we just go through it very quickly, because there weren't too many.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 you made what I would call a change, I don't know if it would be substantial, but you can tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The change in paragraph 1 is more of a technical nature. It's not linked to the case, but it is linked to the institution that I attended, that is, which military academy I was enrolled in.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So that's not substantial, you agree. Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, in the original translation it said that I had joined the Territorial Defence. But I applied to the Territorial Defence, which in my opinion is different; and upon that I was assigned to the exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just keep it to the changes. Like, for instance, paragraph 3, "We had joined." And am I correct if I say that you changed it to "registered"? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So we won't go into the details. Then we move on to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the position of Mr. Salko Beba was called "deputy commander." He was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good. So you changed "deputy" to "assistant." Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, I underlined the word "assistant" and "security." And I explained to you what the point was in the presence of an interpreter. I explained it in my mother tongue, in Bosnian, saying that I did not have a regular position designated by establishment as an assistant deputy. So I couldn't be the assistant of the deputy commander because I wasn't appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 29, line 20 my learned friend said that the witness declared that he didn't join but that he registered. The witness never said that he joined or that he registered but that he applied. In other words, he placed himself at the disposal of the TO and was then appointed to the exchange commission. So for the benefit of the transcript, I think it needs to be corrected because what I heard in my own language does not correspond to what my learned friend said in English in the line that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can have the witness explain this point fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, because the witness was at the proofing along with the interpreter and we know exactly what he said and he knows, and we made the corrections and he made it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could you tell us, we had the word "joined." Could you tell us what word you corrected it with for us.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the 19th April, 2004 did you use the word "applied"?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I wrote it down as a correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks. Then we move on to clause 4. And I'd ask the Court to bear with me, because we don't have too many. Then we move on to clause 4. Could you tell us what you corrected in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part of the statement, that is, in paragraph 4, I underlined the word "assistant" and the word "security." And I explained to representatives of the OTP that I assisted Mr. Beba Salko but I didn't have a fully regulated position in the operations group on the basis of an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And would by correct if I got it right when I said -- when I wrote that you said you just performed the duties, you didn't have a rank? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then we go to paragraph 7, which is one of the most important paragraphs in this statement. And could you tell the Trial Chamber or show the Trial Chamber the changes that you made to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In line 5, it said that it was "attached to" the operations group, and I changed it to being "part of" the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that that was the only correction in paragraph 7 of the statement? Am I correct? So could you answer for the benefit of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So would I be correct in saying that up until the 19th of April, 2004 you had agreed with the comment made in paragraph 7 that you were a member of the military service -- Security Service, that you were part of the OG? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that I was a member of the Military Security. I explained that I had an official ID and for what period of time. That is undisputed --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Eminovic, at this point in time the process is just for us to make sure that the corrections that you made and what was there, if it's what you stand by. And you haven't changed anything in that paragraph other than the fact to what you said. So we are taking it that that is what you mean. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And then we go on to paragraph 14, because that's the other one that reflects a change. And could you tell us--

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to draw attention to the fact that the Trial Chamber has in fact ruled that the Prosecution should be allowed to examine the witness in this way to clarify certain facts, but this is the second time when the witness is trying to explain something my learned friend is interrupting him, so that we will not be able to hear what the witness wants to say. So I think he should be allowed to finish his sentence instead of being interrupted, as he was on page 32, lines 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, what were you going to add concerning paragraph 7? Because the Defence believes that you were interrupted. Did you have anything more to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say, Madam Prosecutor said that I was a member of the Military Security Service of the operations group. It doesn't say that I was a member of the operations group but that I was a member of the Military Security Service. And I have said in my testimony that I did have an official ID of the Military Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, this procedure at the moment is just for us to go through your corrections that you made to the statement, and the next process will be the questioning part. So if we could leave all the comments for then, I'll be happy. Let's go on -- we're just highlighting the changes, to show the character -- if in fact the statement was in fact so changed. Could we go to number 16 on your B/C/S statement. Did you have a change?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a change in paragraph 8 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is one you made. So could you tell --

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preliminary translation, it was stated that the 3rd Corps had a prisoners centre in the basement of the barracks, but the correction is that the operations group had a temporary detention or detention-on-remand facility in the basement of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word in B/C/S is "pritvor," as opposed to "zatvor."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And we have one at paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the earlier version, it was stated that I am aware that HVO and BH army prisoners were detained in cells at the same time, sometimes separately. But the correction was that every effort was made for them to be separate. And I think that during the proofing we agreed that the English version was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, we agreed it was correct. And did we have a correction in number 17?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instead of the word "prison" the word "detention" should be put, the last word in paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we go to paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We just did 16, if --

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to 17.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one-but-last sentence in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: There's one correction you will have noticed, one word. Could you just tell us what was the correction for the one word, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original translation, it said "I knew one of those criminals who beat him and I somehow managed to stop them." The correction was "I knew one of those men."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. 19?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, in the original translation it said "While I was working in the Security Service I learnt that houses in Guca Gora had been looted and set on fire when the ABiH army had taken control of the village." In the corrected version, instead of the word "I learnt" or "I was aware," the word "heard" should be put, "I heard."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the part of the sentence that "The ABiH army took control of the village" is underlined and two question marks are put there. During the proofing, we discussed this point. And I told you that this related to what I saw when I was in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we'll move to number 26. We're almost done. And there was one word there.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, the second sentence, in the original translation it said, "I think that no investigation was carried out against soldiers of the 3rd Corps." The correction is the following: "I don't know whether there was an investigation."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, number 27, the last one.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the translation, the word "Bermudas" was used, and we corrected this to "shorter trousers." We agreed on that. And the word "usually" in the next sentence was deleted, so what remains is "They didn't have badges."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that the statement in English given by you on the 11th and the 14th of November, 2003 and the B/C/S version that you read on the 19th of April, 2003 has not changed substantially or didn't change in any way from when you gave the statement? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as the witness has clarified everything, in paragraph 27 there's another sentence that has been underlined. Could the witness tell us what this means, as he has clarified some other underlinings that he did. And I also think that the Trial Chamber was able to hear what substantial changes have been made in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I happened to be at the proofing along with the interpreter and the investigator and the witness, and even though it's -- something is underlined there, the only point the witness made was with respect to Bermuda shorts. And the English version had three-quarter-leg shorts, and we assured him that that was what was written in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Am I correct, Mr. Eminovic? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we discussed the next underlined sentence as well, because it is slightly in collision with what was said earlier on. So we did discuss this, especially the part of the sentence that reads "After their shifts on the front, they did come and go but I don't know where they came and -- came from and went to."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you proofed with the Prosecution on the 19th of April and you made the corrections, with respect to paragraph 7 did you speak to the Prosecution with respect to the way we describe the shorts? You said you had a problem with it because it said "Bermuda shorts." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: All right. And then we drew your attention to the fact that the English version did not have "Bermuda shorts"; it had "three-quarter-leg shorts," as you were saying. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good. You underlined one - one, two, three, four, five - the fifth and part of the sixth line, but did you indicate to us and the interpreter that you wanted to change that or you had a problem? Because we don't have any changes. And as far as I can recall, the only issue with the 27 was the Bermuda shorts.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also a problem over the word "usually," not just "the Bermuda shorts," but also the next sentence, the word "usually," the first word in the B/C/S. We crossed it out. And then we also spoke about this sentence that "They came to town from their shifts walking around and scaring people." I said that, in principle, I cannot say that they came from the front because I don't know where they came from nor where they went.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And is that your only correction?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we go to the issue of the Travnik barracks, please. It has been established from your evidence this morning that you were involved in writing military orders and were a part of the OG, so to speak. And my question to you is: In that capacity, did you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has never said that he was a member of the OG. He repeated time and again that he was in the Military Security that, he had a military ID and helped Salko Beba. I don't know why the colleague has been insisting on the fact that he was a member of the OG, but he has never said that he had been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will assess this issue, whether he was de jure or de facto member of the OG. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Eminovic, for clarification for everybody, which Military Security Service do you refer to when you say "we were both members of the Military Security Service"? What are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are speaking to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps, which issued the official ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So that was the Military Secret Service of the 3rd Corps, of which you were a member; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not secret. It was the Military Security Service --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think we have a -- something wrong there. But it's the Military Security Service. Where does the OG come in in respect to the Military Security Service? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that question. In what sense the operations group?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You see, if you look at paragraph 7 of your statement - and I read - "Beba and I were both members of the Military Security Service. Beba reported directly to Alagic. It was also -- he was also supposed to report to the ABiH 3rd Corps security commander, who I think was Ramiz Dugalic. At the time, Beba was responsible for a company of 40 to 50 military police attached to the OG." Could you help us, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Salko Beba was officially appointed assistant of the commander for military security, and he was responsible to Mr. Alagic and horizontally, he was responsible to the assistant commander for security in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And it is your statement that this does not have any part to do with the OG; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not claiming that. I'm claiming that Mr. Salko was directly responsible to Commander Alagic in the sense of duties pertaining to military security in the area of responsibility of the OG and, horizontally speaking, responsible to the assistant commander of the 3rd Corps for security matters. So he was responsible to Commander Alagic and he sent out information to the security bodies of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. We will leave this for the Chamber to decide. But you will agree with me that you did assist in the drafting of military orders and taking statements and receiving reports, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in taking statements regarding circumstances surrounding war crimes. Those statements were taken in the premises of the exchange prisoners commission, and most of them were taken from the expelled population from the territory of Bosanska Krajina. I helped Salko Beba and I wrote orders on the basis of instructions received.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is my question: In doing such, did you receive any reports with respect to HVO prisoners or Croats or any of the like?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 18 of your statement. And I would briefly read it for you: "I had him taken from the cells to Beba in my office, where I spoke to him about war crimes and his motivation for having the ear. He told me that the HVO was offering a bounty of 200 DM for the ears of dead ABiH soldiers. I took a short statement from him about war crimes. I made sure that he was kept in a separate cell because I was aware that his life was in danger. I know that he was detained at the barracks for several months. Someone from the criminal investigation department took a more detailed statement from him later. I know that the ICRC was informed of his detention because the ICRC officer from Zenica came to visit him." Is it your evidence that when -- or rather, may I ask you this: What was the contents of these statements that you took? What was told to you by these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I said that I took statements only from one person, Mr. Bonic Krunoslav, because by chance I found myself at Beba's office and there was no one to do the job. I talked to him about what he had done, and I bore in mind that it was a 16-year-old boy and someone who had decided to do something of the sort to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. The question was not what you decided to do but what was reported to you. What did you take in these statements?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bonic told me that he had been captured between the lines of the ABiH army and the HVO in the area of Puticevo and that at some public gathering in Vitez Mario Cerkez had promised every HVO soldier bringing an ear would be rewarded with 200 Deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything about his physical condition and how he was treated?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I saw that he had received several blows, and I tried to have this person no longer be subjected to such treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So with respect to Mr. Bonic, at least that is one individual that you know was subjected to beatings; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now I will ask you to look at paragraph 15 of your statement. And it says - and I read - "The military police guarding the prisoners were unable to prevent soldiers coming into the cells and beating prisoners. People in the barracks were talking about the beatings. I know that Beba spoke to his counterparts in the 17th Krajina Brigade about this in an attempt to stop it." Did you receive any evidence or any notice or were you ever told or did you know of any beatings that took place in the Travnik basement?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, I heard about those events, but the only time I eyewitnessed this was in the case of Mr. Bonic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Beba's office that you visited at least twice weekly, could you tell us where it was located.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The small building approximately straight, once you get past the entrance of the barracks, after the ambulance, the first aid, and a little bit to the right. Behind that building, to the right, the service -- car service is located. In that building. And from the entrance to that -- to reach that building you had to pass through a small park.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us on your weekly trips if you had ever been to the Travnik barracks.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That building where Mr. Salko had his office was within the barracks. And there were several buildings within the premises of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So I'm correct in saying that Mr. Salko Beba's office was within the barracks; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you visited there twice a week; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, during your performance of your duties as a Military Security Service, that part of it when you wore the military uniform, you had to go to the monastery; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber today when you got to the monastery what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I reached the monastery, I saw some graffiti in the Arabic language. I saw some bullet holes on a statue which was in the compound of the monastery. I saw members of the 306th Brigade securing the monastery. And they were there and protected the monastery with sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And is that the only thing you saw?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the monastery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about outside?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside I saw two or three houses from which smoke was coming out and from Travnik and Guca Gora we saw that the HVO positions had opened fire --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think you misunderstood the question. Outside of the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the monastery, at its entrance there were several soldiers of the 306th Brigade. I don't remember if it was the military police or someone else, but they belonged to the 306th Brigade and they were securing the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to read paragraph 21 for you of your statement: "Several 306th Military Police had set up sandbags on the road at the entrance to Guca Gora. Beba and I went to the monastery. Several 306th soldiers were at the monastery gate. There was a priest but no soldiers in the monastery grounds. I saw a lot of Arab graffiti on the outside walls and some bullet holes in a statue in the garden." Could you assist us with--

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know what needs to be clarified here. What has been read by the learned friend has been already said by the witness in response to her questions. And before putting the question, he had already mentioned that he had seen the graffiti and bullet holes on a statue in front of the monastery. I don't know what the -- what is being asked of the witness, 42, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the purpose of question? Well, he answered the question about the graffiti yesterday. I don't believe at any point he mentioned that he had seen bullet holes -- bullet holes. Perhaps that may be the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is just the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you explain to us if in fact you did see bullet holes and what other things you may have seen, please.

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I saw bullet holes on the statue in this part. I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you went to the cell at the Travnik barracks, you saw Bonic being beaten. So you were down in the cells, were you?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in the cell. I was in the corridor of the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you saw -- you were in the corridor of the detention centre, and you saw Mr. Bonic being beaten; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Is there any other thing that you would like to tell this Trial Chamber that you would have seen then?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a soldier who had hit -- been hitting Bonic a number of times, and when I insisted, he stopped. Everyone was shocked when they saw that a child of 16 cut other people's ears off.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: "Everyone was shocked." "Everyone" meaning what? What did you see down in that basement? Did you see other prisoners? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several members of the army that had captured Bonic and the police that were securing the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Is it your evidence to this Court that Bonic was the only person in that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: JASENKO EMINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. I'm saying that I could see that these people were shocked, because they were -- found themselves in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. I am not disputing the fact that people were shocked about whatever. I'm asking you just to tell the Court when you went down in the corridors of the Travnik detention centre, as you would like to call it, what did you see in what were the conditions? What did you see in whom did you see? You saw Bonic being beaten. Did you see anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in conformity with the rules of hostile witnesses, the colleague has asked questions.
